body.translated_text: Om, homage to the Omniscient One!

children.translated_text: He who, having realized the ultimate truth, was indeed the glorious <s>Ghanavyūha</s>,
who became <s>Śvetaketu</s> for the benefit of the beings in <s>Tuṣita</s>,
and then became <s>Śākyaketu</s> for the welfare of the world here,
may he be victorious — the conqueror of death, who has displayed infinite miraculous powers!
Having attained the state of freedom from aging and death,
the cause of freedom from aging and death,
for the attainment of freedom from aging and death,
having bowed with devotion to the Perfectly Awakened One,
difficult to comprehend for those of dull intellect,
difficult to accomplish for those of wavering minds,
the effective method of cheating death,
in accordance with the scriptures, is here expounded.
The complete cheating of death
is possible only for the liberated ones.
For all the unliberated,
it is merely a delay for some time.
The cessation of life-force, senses, and mind
is the characteristic of death.
The prolongation of life through skillful means
is called the cheating of death.
As long as one lives in <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence),
practicing the <s>Dharma</s> with senses controlled,
for that long one produces the accumulation of merit and other requisites
that accomplish <s>Bodhi</s> (awakening).
Apart from life, nothing of essence
is seen in <s>saṃsāra</s>.
Therefore, by various means, one should swiftly
undertake the cheating of death.
Nothing is difficult
when skillful means are properly applied.
The efficacy of gems, <s>mantras</s>, and herbs
is universally acknowledged.
Having recognized death from afar by its signs,
the appropriate countermeasure should be applied.
When death has already struck like a thunderbolt,
what can even the wisest person do?
The signs of death are of two kinds,
distinguished as external and internal.
By them, impending death
is known by those devoted to the subject.
If someone desires to ascertain
the signs of death,
one should do so while in good health;
otherwise there is uncertainty.
Due to imbalance of the <s>dhātus</s> (bodily elements), due to disease,
due to the effect of cataracts and such conditions,
due to the power of fear, grief, and the like,
appearances may differ from the norm.
From disturbances of divine, elemental, and both kinds,
death has three types of signs.
Since the arising of the ominous sign depends on attaining it,
one should identify it by its specific type.
Divine disturbance is of two kinds,
distinguished as external and internal.
Elemental disturbance is also twofold —
one should determine it in the same way.
Death from divine disturbance
is called <s>ādhidaivika</s> (caused by fate).
Divine disturbance includes fasting and such,
and is characterized by lightning strikes and the like.
Death from elemental disturbance
is called <s>ādhibhautika</s> (caused by elements).
Elemental disturbance is <s>pitta</s> (bile) and such,
and calamities of fire, water, and the like.
Death from both kinds of disturbance
is said to be born of both.
The combined disturbance is of lightning etc.
and afflictions of <s>pitta</s>, <s>śleṣma</s> (phlegm), etc.
Since the ominous signs are infinite,
their simultaneous occurrence is not considered possible.
Even sequentially, not all of them appear,
but rather in numbers of one or more.
Where death is observed without seeing the sign,
the fault lies in the determination there,
not in the non-existence of the sign.
[This means the observer failed, not the system.]
Where the sign is observed but death is not seen,
in that case, if there is no error,
one should posit an intervening obstacle
such as <s>Dharma</s> practice and the like.
When death has been ascertained from afar,
there will be great benefit,
for one can engage in renunciation to the extent of one's ability
and in the application of countermeasures.
Being always composed,
with mind single-pointedly focused on this matter,
one should first observe
the external signs.
The time for ascertaining the signs
is considered to be of two kinds:
fixed and unfixed —
this should be known with diligence.
At the <s>saṃkrānti</s> (solstice), full moon, and such occasions,
consisting of moments such as dawn and the like,
the time is called fixed;
unfixed is the opposite of that.
A cheek with throbbing joints may occur
excessively from the perception of death,
but also from contact with wind, cold, and the like —
therefore it should be distinguished separately.
<s>Karkaṭa</s> (Cancer) is the zodiac sign, <s>Āṣāḍha</s> is the month;
<s>Puṣya</s> corresponds to <s>Makara</s> (Capricorn).
In <s>Karkaṭa</s> and <s>Makara</s>,
the sign of death manifests.
On the day of the <s>Āṣāḍha</s> solstice,
at midday, the foot-measure
of the shadow of one standing facing north
should be the natural one.
On the day of the <s>Puṣya</s> solstice,
that same shadow should be seven feet.
The observation of the shadow should be at midday
under a cloudless sky.
Each month there is an increase of one foot,
each month a decrease of one foot.
If there is any deviation from this,
the suspicion of death arises.
There should be an increase of one foot each month
from <s>Āṣāḍha</s> until <s>Makara</s>.
There should be a decrease of one foot each month
from <s>Makara</s> until <s>Karkaṭa</s>.
From <s>Āṣāḍha</s>, the increase proceeds in order;
from <s>Puṣya</s>, the decrease proceeds in order likewise.
Having observed the deviation of the shadow,
one should predict the months until death.
If there is increase during the time of decrease,
or decrease during the time of increase,
from that very time,
death is certain within a month.
Even during the time of increase, if there is excessive increase,
affliction from various diseases results.
Even during the time of decrease, if there is excessive decrease,
death itself is certain, without doubt.
At the end of <s>Āṣāḍha</s> and <s>Puṣya</s>,
and before <s>Karkaṭa</s> and <s>Matsya</s> (Pisces),
the six days in each case
serve for determining timely and untimely death.
By the days at the end of <s>Āṣāḍha</s>,
the auspicious and inauspicious for <s>Śrāvaṇa</s> etc. are determined.
By the remaining days of <s>Puṣya</s>,
the auspicious and inauspicious for <s>Māgha</s> etc. are determined.
If, having pierced the soles of the feet,
the pricking sensation reaches the navel,
after three days and nights,
death occurs.
If, having pierced the soles of the feet,
it also pierces the eyes,
then after three months,
one goes to the abode of <s>Yama</s> (Death).
If, having pierced the soles of the feet,
it pierces the nose,
then within three days, certainly,
one goes to death alone.
If, at the time of urination and defecation,
there is simultaneous sneezing,
at that very moment,
death comes within a year for that person.
From piercing at the tip of the nose,
death occurs within five years.
From non-perception of the tip of the tongue,
death occurs within three days for men.
Death occurs within four months
from a sharp piercing at the tip of the ear.
Immediate death certainly occurs
from piercing at the <s>ūrṇā</s> spot (between the eyebrows).
When piercing occurs simultaneously
in the moon and sun [left and right nostrils],
then death occurs within a month;
therefore one should earn merit.
If, during sexual intercourse,
sneezing occurs at the beginning, middle, and end
equally, then within
five months, one goes to death.
If the joints of the little fingers
of both hands and feet
are pierced simultaneously for someone,
that person dies within a month.
When piercing occurs simultaneously
between the heart and the throat,
death comes within three fortnights
if one does not practice the <s>Dharma</s>.
When the three palates are pierced
simultaneously and repeatedly,
death comes within three days
even if one were equal to <s>Śakra</s> (Indra).
One who cannot see in a mirror
the reflection of the pupil of the left eye
will certainly die within seven days
if there is no countermeasure.
If during sexual union
the sound of a bell is heard in the ears,
death comes within three months
even if one were equal to <s>Brahmā</s>.
If the semen becomes black
on the first day of the bright fortnight,
death comes within six months;
red indicates disease.
At the base of the ear, between the eyebrows,
and at the crown of the head, separately,
if there is piercing without a countermeasure,
death occurs immediately.
Beginning from the big toe,
if a burning piercing sensation extends
up to the navel, that person
will certainly die within six months.
From the big toe to the heart,
then to the throat or head,
death comes after three months, three fortnights,
or one day, respectively.
From loosening of the flesh at the tip of the nose,
death occurs within seven nights.
From deterioration of the flesh of the cheeks,
death occurs within five months.
If no pulsation is seen
between the eyes and the nose,
knowing death comes within five days,
one should take up the provisions of <s>Dharma</s>.
If the pupils of the eyes suddenly
become dim,
death comes within six months
if no countermeasure is applied.
If suddenly the nose becomes crooked,
the ears shift from their position,
and the eyes become round,
death is indicated within seven days.
If the heart suddenly becomes depressed,
death comes within a fortnight.
From the severing of the channels on the sides of the neck,
also within a fortnight.
If suddenly a black line appears
in the middle of the tongue,
or the teeth clamp tightly,
then death comes within two nights.
From the observation of the severing of the channel
behind the ear conch,
death comes on that very day
or within five days.
If nails that are red in color
suddenly become pale,
death comes within six months
if one does not perform <s>mantras</s> and such practices.
One who suddenly becomes fat,
or emaciated, angry, and terror-stricken —
death comes within a year for that person
if one does not practice the <s>Dharma</s>.
When the senses no longer apprehend
their respective objects,
when speech frequently stumbles,
and mental confusion occurs repeatedly —
when the eyes constantly stream,
when there is confusion even regarding seen forms,
when one cannot see one's own reflection
in a mirror or in water —
if one sees a rainbow at night,
or the constellation of stars by day,
if one sees lightning without clouds
flashing in the southern direction —
if one sees the shadow-path by day,
or the falling of a meteor,
if one sees a gathering in one place
of geese, crows, and peacocks —
if one sees two moons, or two suns,
or one's own head ablaze,
if one sees a <s>gandharva</s> city (mirage)
atop a tree or mountain peak —
if one sees <s>pretas</s> (hungry ghosts) and <s>piśācas</s> (demons)
and other terrifying beings invisible to others,
and trembles violently,
or frequently falls into a swoon —
if one's vomit, urine, or feces
have the luster of gold or silver,
seeing each of these separately,
death comes within a month.
If one perceives cuts in the throat, lips, palate, and tongue,
and holes in the body likewise,
death is certain for that person
within six months.
The throat, lips, palate, tongue,
and teeth of one who
dry out repeatedly — within six months,
one should predict that person's death.
Non-perception at night of the constellation circle,
the Seven Sages (Ursa Major), and the directions,
indicates death within seven days;
or spontaneous flames appearing on the body.
<s>Arundhatī</s>, <s>Rohiṇī</s>,
<s>Dhruva</s> (the Pole Star), and the shadow-path likewise —
if one suddenly cannot see them at night,
one should predict death within six months.
If one sees the moon without its dark spot,
or the sun without its rays,
or the sun with rays [when it should not have them],
or the moon also with rays —
the sun at night, the moon by day,
or one's own eyes ablaze,
a star as large as <s>Meru</s>,
or the ocean like a river —
hiccups at the navel, sneezing at the anus,
a lotus-like complexion on the face,
red pustules on the throat,
variegation of color on the body —
weeping with tears arising from the heart,
trembling also in the palate,
a moonbeam feeling like fire-touch,
a sunbeam feeling cold as snow —
a hole in the moon, a hole in the sun,
holes in the earth and in the sky —
one who sees these by oneself
should expect death within a fortnight.
If urine, semen, and feces
are discharged simultaneously,
death comes within a year;
the countermeasure is medicines and such.
If half of the body is cold
and the other half is hot,
death comes within seven nights;
one should contemplate the next world.
If the 'ha' sound feels cold
and the 'phu' sound feels like fire —
one who experiences this
will see <s>Yama</s> (Death) within ten days.
When a black line is seen
at the base of the ring fingers,
death comes after eighteen days
due to the fault of previous <s>karma</s>.
If a three-colored lizard
swiftly climbs upon one's head,
death for that person
is certain within five months.
If no sound is produced from the body
when wiped with the hands,
along with coldness of all limbs,
death is certain within ten days.
If the arms and shanks swing out simultaneously
when one walks,
and the sacred thread breaks,
death comes for that person within one year.
If in mud or a dusty area,
in front or behind,
the footprint upon stepping is incomplete or diminished,
death comes within four months.
If one suddenly sees a person
of dark-tawny color,
death comes after three years
if it is not ascribed to delusion.
Death comes within two months if the heart and feet
dry immediately after bathing.
Death comes within three nights if
a foul odor arises and the form becomes distorted.
On the day of the sun in the donkey asterism, with waters
filling the cavity of the mouth,
blowing out daily,
gradually [observing] what is situated in the middle of that
one should see a wondrous rainbow;
such a person always has long life.
One who does not see it [has] six months of life remaining —
such is the diversity of <s>karma</s>.
On a Sunday with a harsh [sun], one should look
ahead into the middle of the sky
[and see forms] like strands of pearl necklaces,
adorned with pearl ornaments,
with the hue of sapphire gems,
shaped like balls of hair,
leaving the visible region
and moving to other places
one should see numerous serpents
as if continuously bound together.
If these are not seen, within six months
death is declared.
In the morning, or in the evening,
or in moonlight, for a long time, facing forward,
having extended both arms, observing one's own shadow,
one should then slowly gaze at the sky.
If a shadow is seen there too,
white and in human form —
from the non-appearance of its head,
death shall occur within a year.
From the non-appearance of the left hand,
the destruction of son and wife shall occur;
from the non-appearance of the right,
[death] of father, brothers, and other elders.
Having placed both arms upon the knees
and formed an <s>añjali</s> (joined palms) upon the head,
one should observe the shadow resembling a plantain fruit
in the middle between those [hands].
When a single petal there
is perceived as opening,
on that very <s>tithi</s> (lunar day), certainly
death shall occur within six months.
When the breath travels through the solar channel,
these three should be observed:
in the ear, in the head, and in the eye —
sound, smoke, and light respectively.
Having firmly closed both ears,
if the deep rumbling sound
is not heard for five days,
or ten, or fifteen,
or up to twenty days,
or twenty-five —
death [occurs] in [respectively] five, four, three, two, or one
year(s), in sequence.
In the intervals between these too,
sixteen days should be calculated,
with quarter-fractions of a year
successively added.
One who does not see a garland of smoke
rising above the head for seven days —
for him there shall be
death within a limit of three years.
In one's own eyes, in the four directions,
by pressing with the fingers,
lights resembling cat's eyes
are seen flickering rapidly.
If these are seen even without pressing,
death shall occur within a hundred days.
This should be known in general terms;
but the specific [signs] are now stated.
Below and above the moon [reflection in the eye],
and near the ear and nose —
when the light disappears, death shall occur
in six, three, two, or one month(s).
If in the sun [reflection] too, the same sequence
as for the moon applies, then as before,
death shall occur in [respectively] ten, five, three, or two
days.
From the reversal of one's own form [reflection],
death shall occur within six months.
From the disappearance of the tip of the nose [reflection],
death shall occur within five months.
From deafness in both ears,
death shall occur after four months.
From the failure of otherwise healthy senses,
death shall occur within three months.
From the non-appearance of light between the eyebrows,
one shall see <s>Yama</s> (Death) within two months.
Death occurs after one month
from the shrinking of the testicles.
From the non-appearance of the reflection
in another's eyes, destruction within a fortnight.
From the tongue being unable to turn back [i.e., reach the palate],
encounter with death within ten days.
From the reversal of the navel [shape],
death approaches within five days.
From the contraction of both sides [of the body],
death shall occur within three days.
From complete stiffness of the entire body,
death shall occur within one day.
From the disappearance of the three lines
on the forehead, death within three days.
If, in a healthy person, the palate and tongue
become insensate and devoid of moisture,
death occurs within five days
or within fifty days.
A sour quality in taste,
a bluish quality in color,
abnormality of semen and urine —
[these indicate] a vision of death within six months.
If one's urine flows simultaneously in five streams,
or spirals to the left, or is foul-smelling —
for him death [shall occur]
within six months.
Whether in the dark or bright
fortnight, if semen is extremely dark,
death within six months; if not,
by that very [method] a remedy is possible.
Abandoning the dark portion
and taking hold of the bright portion,
when the wind blows in the lunar [channel],
the remedy shall come from entering [that channel].
Even though one's own body is steady,
if its shadow is trembling,
death shall occur within four months —
so say those skilled in the <s>āgamas</s> (scriptures).
If one sees one's own shadow
gone to the southern direction,
'This very day is our death' —
thus one should contemplate impermanence.
Being meaningless, contradictory,
and manifesting falsity and so forth,
dreams too are untrue for everyone —
therefore faith [in them] is not proper.
A dream shown by a deity,
or a person whose dreams are [always] true —
such a one, having placed confidence in the dream,
should observe the signs of death [therein].
A <s>kiṃśuka</s> tree, a <s>kovidāra</s> tree,
or a flowering <s>karavīra</s> (oleander) —
whoever climbs these at the end of a dream,
his death shall occur within six months.
A person who in a dream climbs
a funeral post,
or a heap of sand or ashes —
his death is as stated before.
One who, mounted on a donkey,
travels toward the southern direction
and does not return —
so too is his life [ended].
And one who, mounted on a monkey,
travels toward the southern direction
and awakens while still there —
death shall occur for him as before.
A man who climbs a staff, or a sacrificial post,
or a memorial pillar,
or an anthill, or a heap of earth —
he shall not live [beyond] six months.
A dark maiden, enraged,
who binds one with bonds —
she should be known as <s>Kālarātrī</s> (Night of Death),
causing death within seven days.
A woman clad in black garments,
dark, who desires a man,
[wearing] an oleander garland in the dream —
he goes to <s>Yama</s>'s (Death's) realm.
If one enters darkness in a dream,
or a pit, or a prison,
or falls from a tree in a dream —
he is situated near death.
One who sees a tree, grass, or wood
that is barren [of fruit]
while sleeping, upon the head or body —
he shall not live [beyond] six months.
A man who, mounted on a chariot drawn by monkeys,
goes toward the eastern direction —
upon waking, he should know:
'This was my last night.'
If one is devoured by dogs, crows, vultures, jackals,
<s>Rakṣas</s> (demons), <s>Pretas</s> (hungry ghosts), and <s>Piśācas</s> (ghouls),
or carried off by
donkeys, pigs, camels, or bulls —
one should certainly declare
death within one year.
The pacification of dream-seen omens
[requires] an understanding [that they are] like illusions.
If, while sleeping, one sees before oneself
a dark man holding an iron rod,
dressed in dark garments —
death is obtained within three months.
With body smeared with red sandal-paste,
adorned with red garlands,
anointed with oil, greatly terrified,
head shaved, wearing red garments —
riding a donkey at speed,
going toward the southern direction —
if one sees oneself thus in a dream,
death [occurs] within six months.
Red garlands and perfumes,
or red garments —
whoever receives these in a dream,
death shall occur within eight months.
The external signs of death
are innumerable — who could
with a single mouth
speak them even in a hundred years?
These external signs
indicating death, as described,
having recognized them, one should quickly
make effort to cheat [death] through <s>mantras</s> (sacred formulae) and other means.
Thus ends the first chapter of the <s>Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa</s> (Instructions on Cheating Death), composed by the learned <s>Vāgīśvarakīrti</s>.
Now the internal signs of death
are clearly described.
These are to be known through the arising of the breath;
the breath operates through the nose and mouth.
From external signs alone,
there is no certain determination of death,
so long as the internal
signs are not definitively ascertained.
From the certainty of both [external and internal signs],
death is determined with full clarity.
In external [signs], error of judgment [may arise]
due to disease and other conditions as well.
At the <s>saṃkrānti</s> (solar transit) of the months beginning with <s>Puṣya</s>,
and on <s>parvans</s> (juncture days) such as the full moon,
the general signs of death
should be observed from morning onward.
On whichever day the examiner
determines the [remaining] time,
from that day death
shall occur after the measured time has elapsed.
For all living beings
of balanced constitution,
in the right and left nostrils
respectively,
the breath flows for half a <s>yāma</s> (watch, ~1.5 hours),
called the solar and lunar [channels].
From the reversal of this [pattern],
the wise should infer death and such [misfortunes].
Beginning from the first day
of the bright [fortnight], the breath flows in the lunar [channel]
for three days,
then in the solar [channel] for three days,
three days again in the lunar,
then three days in the solar —
by this sequence, invariably,
until the fifteenth of the bright [fortnight].
Likewise, beginning from the dark [fortnight],
the breath flows in the solar [channel]
for three days as before,
until the other fifteenth [day].
From the definitely ascertained reversal
of this sequence for three fortnights,
death shall occur within six months —
one should then remember <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) alone.
From the reversal of two fortnights,
misfortune to friends and kinsmen shall occur.
From the reversal of one fortnight,
a severe illness shall arise.
If the breath flows in reverse
for one, two, three, four, five,
or six days, then
quarrels, disturbances, and such arise.
The breath may travel through the three channels
due to departure from natural [flow];
[if it flows through the central channel] past midday, death [ensues]
if no remedy is applied.
If the breath, without transition,
flows through both channels
for ten days —
he shall die at the [next] <s>saṃkrānti</s> (solar transit).
At the moment of the equinox,
if both eyes of a person tremble,
one should know his destruction [will come]
within a day and night — there is no doubt.
If the breath flows here and there
in many ways for half a <s>prahara</s> (watch),
one should know for that person
[there will be] honor and gain.
If the breath, having passed the five [days of]
<s>saṃkrānti</s>, flows through the mouth —
for that person there shall be loss of wealth,
or agitation, or fear and such.
If the breath flows through the left nostril,
having passed thirteen
<s>saṃkrāntis</s> (solar transits) —
for that person illness and such shall arise.
When, abandoning both nostrils,
[the breath] goes through the mouth,
that is the [last] day of his life,
even if he be as [strong as] a thunderbolt.
Beginning from the <s>saṃkrānti</s> of the month of <s>Mārgaśīrṣa</s>,
if the breath
flows in the solar [channel] for five days,
death [occurs] in eighteen years.
Beginning from the <s>saṃkrānti</s> of the month of <s>Aśvayuj</s>,
if the breath
flows [in the solar channel] for five days, death
shall occur in fifteen years.
If likewise in [the month of] <s>Śrāvaṇa</s>,
death in twelve years.
If likewise in [the month of] <s>Jyeṣṭha</s>,
death shall occur in nine years.
Beginning from the <s>saṃkrānti</s> of the month of <s>Caitra</s>,
if the breath flows [in the solar channel]
for five days, death
shall then occur in six years.
From the <s>saṃkrānti</s> of the month of <s>Māgha</s>,
if the breath flows [in the solar channel] for five days,
death after three years —
so say those skilled in [determining] time.
Everywhere, if the breath flows
for two, three, or four days [instead of five],
those should be adjusted by fractions of a year
properly in order.
If the breath flows likewise in the lunar [channel instead],
one is free from death, [but]
disease, famine, wilderness [hardship],
grief, royal [persecution], and other calamities [may occur].
This clear awareness of the general time [of death]
has been presented.
For awareness of the specific time,
another approach is now shown.
When the sun is in the seventh sign [from the birth sign]
and the moon is in the birth constellation —
that time is called <s>Pauṣṇa</s>,
and it determines [the time of] death.
From the sign in which a person was born,
that which is the seventh from it
is known as <s>samasapta</s> (the seventh sign);
the sun positioned there is called <s>samasaptaga</s> (gone to the seventh).
If in that very sign the moon
is in the birth <s>nakṣatra</s> (constellation),
that time should be known as the <s>Pauṣṇa</s> period;
therein death is to be examined.
The learned one should always determine the time
when the continuously-flowing [breath] enters
the solar channel;
at other times it is an improper time [for examination].
At whatever moment a different course
of the breath arises,
at the completion of that moment,
death [is certain] — there is no doubt here.
If during the <s>Pauṣṇa</s> period the breath flows
in the solar [channel] for half a day,
one should predict death
in years numbered as fourteen.
If it flows for one day, for a full day-and-night,
for two, three, or four days —
[death occurs] in [respectively] twelve, ten, eight,
six, or four years, in sequence.
If it flows for five days, for ten days,
or for fifteen days —
death shall occur in [respectively] three, two, or one year(s)
in sequence.
If the breath flows in the same manner
for twenty or twenty-five [days],
death occurs in six months or three months
respectively, in corresponding order.
If it flows for twenty-six, twenty-seven, twenty-eight,
or twenty-nine days,
death comes in two months, one month, a fortnight,
and ten days, respectively, in order.
If for thirty, thirty-one,
or thirty-two days,
death comes in five, three, or two days
respectively, in corresponding order.
If the breath flows through the solar [nostril]
for up to thirty-three days,
death comes on that very day,
even for <s>Viṣṇu</s> — there is no doubt.
Between the fifth and twenty-fifth days,
the sixteen days
that have not been mentioned —
their calculation is now stated.
If six days, then [death comes] in three years
minus twenty-four [days];
if seven days, then in three years
minus double the previously stated [amount];
if eight days, then in three years
minus seventy-two days;
if nine days, then in three years
minus ninety-six days;
if the breath flows through the solar [nostril]
for eleven days,
death occurs in two years
minus twenty-four nights;
if twelve days, then in two years
minus double the previously stated;
if thirteen days, then in two years
minus seventy-two days;
if fourteen days, then in two years
minus ninety-six days;
if flowing for sixteen days,
then in one year minus twelve [days];
if the breath flows through the solar [nostril] alone
for seventeen days,
death is declared to occur in one year
minus twenty-four days;
if eighteen days, then in one year
minus thirty-six days;
if nineteen days, then in [one year]
minus forty-eight days;
if twenty-one days, then in six months
minus six days;
if twenty-two days, then in six months
minus twelve days;
if flowing for twenty-three days,
then [in six months] minus eighteen days;
if flowing for twenty-four days,
then [in six months] minus twenty-four days;
Thus, within these thirty-three days,
the signs of death arise;
they are to be known according to the arising of the breath,
and not beyond, since [such duration] is impossible.
And here it is also said:

children.text: ādau kṛtvā dinārdhaṃ sakaladinam athā-harniśaṃ yāvad eva
children.translated_text: Beginning with half a day, then a full day, then extending through a day-and-night,

children.text: tasmād ahnor dvayaṃ ca tridinam atha catur-vāsarān vyāpya yāvat
children.translated_text: thence for two days, and for three, and covering four days successively —

children.text: prāṇo nāḍyāśrito yo vahati dinapater udgame savyahīne
children.translated_text: the <s>prāṇa</s> (breath) that flows from a <s>nāḍī</s> (channel) at the rising of the sun, through the left [nostril] being absent —

children.text: tasmin vijñeyam etad bhuvanaravidiśo maṅgalaṃ ṣaṭ catuṣkam
children.translated_text: in that, one should know the auspicious set of six times four, [pertaining to] the directions of the world-illuminating [sun].
From five to twenty-five days the course increases by increments of five;

children.text: tasmād ekottareṇa triguṇitadaśakaṃ tryuttaraṃ yāvad eva
children.translated_text: from that, by increments of one, up to three times ten plus three;

children.text: kāle pauṣṇe samās tās trinayanaśaśinaḥ ṣaṭtriyugmendavo ye
children.translated_text: in the <s>Pauṣṇa</s> period, those [intervals] equal [the months of] the three-eyed one (<s>Śiva</s>), the moon — six, three, two [months], and [the lunar periods];
those months, then the remaining days — [calculated by] the digits of <s>tithi</s> (lunar day), direction, arrow, quality, and two moons — [these are] of life.
Having drawn a <s>tripuṭa</s> (triple-circle) diagram
with thirty-seven cells,
one should write the days of lifespan
and of the <s>prāṇavāyu</s> (life-breath) in numerical order.

children.text: ity āntarāṇy api mayā kathitāni mṛtyor
children.translated_text: Thus the internal signs of death
— also called <s>ariṣṭa</s> (omens of death) by another name —
have been described by me; having recognized them, one should immediately
make effort to cheat death through <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) and other [practices].
Thus ends the second chapter in the <s>Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa</s> (Instructions on Cheating Death) composed by the learned <s>Paṇḍita Vāgīśvarakīrti</s>.
Having recognized the cluster of <s>ariṣṭas</s> (death-omens),
both external and internal,
the collection of methods for cheating [death],
both external and internal, should be known.
The external [method works] through actions of body and speech;
the internal, through meditative practices;
the external, through gems, <s>mantras</s>, and herbs;
the internal, through the powers of <s>yoga</s>.
The cheating of death can be accomplished
by those who undertake it with faith;
therefore one should make one's faith firm,
otherwise there would be only futile exertion.
The subtle <s>dharma</s> cannot be attained
through manifold bodily austerities,
nor through heaps of wealth,
by those devoid of faith — not even by the gods.
Faith is <s>dharma</s>, the supremely subtle;
faith is knowledge, austerity, and oblation;
faith is heaven and liberation;
faith is this entire world.
If one were to give away everything, including one's very life,
without faith,
one would not obtain any fruit whatsoever;
therefore one should be faithful.
First, one should be devoted to <s>dharma</s>
out of the wish to cheat death;
for <s>dharma</s> protects from death,
and death is cheated by <s>dharma</s>.
One should not remain devoid of <s>dharma</s>
even for a single moment, through carelessness;
for even <s>Brahmā</s> himself, without <s>dharma</s>,
is not capable of cheating death.
The <s>dharma</s> approved by the wise is:
truth, generosity, austerity, patience;
and especially, for those who possess compassion,
what need is there for elaborate [discussions of] <s>dharma</s>?
Those whose hearts perpetually overflow
with compassion toward all beings —
for them, knowledge and liberation [come naturally];
what need have they for elaborate [discussions of] <s>dharma</s>?
<s>Ahiṃsā</s> (non-violence) is the supreme <s>dharma</s>,
accepted by all philosophical systems;
for one who constantly practices it,
death gradually recedes far away.
Even one of short lifespan would immediately become long-lived
by saving the lives of
birds, fish, deer, wild animals,
thieves, and others condemned to death.
Even one of long lifespan would immediately become short-lived
by killing
thieves, fish, deer, wild animals,
birds, and others who cling to life.
Through abandoning the ten unwholesome actions,
through taking refuge in the Three Jewels,
and through undertaking the five or eight precepts,
death becomes far removed.
One who rescues those in prison,
those afflicted by severe illness, and those stricken with fear
would surely become long-lived
and a cheater of death.
By giving desired objects
to the destitute, the helpless, the ashamed,
and also respectfully to the virtuous,
one's lifespan certainly increases.
Through reverence for mother, father, teacher, elders,
those advanced in knowledge, and the aged,
and through offerings of respect and honor,
death does not even approach.
Through reverently seeing and bowing daily
in the morning to one's chosen deity
and to those who bear the marks of devotion to that deity,
increase of lifespan is obtained.
By offering bricks and the like
for broken and crumbling <s>caityas</s> (sacred monuments),
even one of short lifespan would become very long-lived,
like an alms-collecting <s>bhikṣu</s> (mendicant).
Through the maintenance of <s>vihāras</s> (monasteries), <s>stūpas</s>, images,
through planting gardens,
and through worship at the eight great [pilgrimage] sites,
one's lifespan always increases.
By feeding the <s>saṃgha</s> (community)
with goods obtained through begging (<s>chandakabhikṣā</s>),
one of seven days' lifespan would become long-lived,
like King <s>Dharmāśoka</s>.
Through making sand <s>caityas</s>,
and through striking the <s>sañcaka</s> (gong),
and through bowing to <s>caityas</s> and the like,
one's lifespan certainly increases.
The <s>Mahāsamāja Sūtra</s>,
the <s>Āṭānāṭīya</s> [<s>Sūtra</s>],
the <s>Kṣudraka</s>, the <s>Mahāmegha</s>,
and the <s>gāthās</s> known as <s>Susvasti</s> —
one should reverently have <s>bhikṣus</s> recite these,
or initiate [the recitation] oneself;
having thus obtained long life,
one becomes a cheater of death.
By single-mindedly and regularly reciting
the <s>Gaṇḍavyūha</s> and other <s>sūtrāntas</s> (scriptures)
that illuminate the <s>Mahāyāna</s>,
one attains the cheating of death.
Through recitation of all the
<s>Yogatantras</s> and other [texts] spoken by the <s>Buddha</s>,
or through the practice of the <s>Pañcarakṣā</s> (Five Protections),
the cheating of death is obtained.
Through the practice of circumambulating
the <s>Uṣṇīṣagarbha Caitya</s> and the like,
and through reciting <s>dhāraṇīs</s> (protective spells),
death is cheated by the diligent.
Through recitation of the <s>Grahādimātṛkā</s> (Planetary Matrix),
preceded by its proper ritual,
and through recitation of the <s>Sahasrāvarta Dhāraṇī</s>
and the <s>Ratnolkā</s> —
the wise, devoted to the recitation of <s>dhāraṇīs</s>
combined with collections of <s>dhāraṇīs</s>,
make even imminent death
become distant.
Through drawing <s>maṇḍalas</s>, through <s>homa</s> (fire oblation),
through the binding of <s>mudrās</s> (ritual gestures),
and through offerings of <s>bali</s> (ritual offerings) and <s>gaṇacakras</s> (feast circles),
[one achieves] the cheating of death.
Through giving food, bedding, and the like
to the noble <s>saṃgha</s> of the four directions,
or even to those who wear merely the saffron robe
around their necks — the cheating of death may result.
Through undertaking such and similar activities,
<s>dharma</s> characterized by merit arises;
from merit, lifespan increases;
from the increase of lifespan, death is cheated.
Thus, <s>dharma</s> has been indicated only briefly;
its elaboration
should be independently drawn out and performed
by those who know how to cheat death.
Having thus become devoted to <s>dharma</s>,
one should ward off death
through accomplished <s>mantras</s>, herbs, and the like,
which produce immediate results.
Through the power of gems, <s>mantras</s>, herbs,
<s>siddha</s> (accomplished) <s>rasāyana</s> (alchemical elixirs),
the defeat of death has been witnessed,
as by <s>siddha vidyādharas</s> (accomplished knowledge-holders).
One who bears a diamond that has passed the examination
described in the <s>Ratnalakṣaṇaśāstra</s> (Treatise on the Characteristics of Gems),
or one who bears a life-prolonging gem,
or one who bears the <s>viśvarūpa</s> (universal-form) [gem] —
the bearer of a priceless sapphire (<s>indranīla</s>)
or of any other great gem
would be a cheater of all [forms of] death —
there is no doubt.
And here, regarding the power of gems,
no reasonable doubt exists,
since it is universally accepted
that gems possess inconceivable powers.
Having performed worship before a sacred image or painting,
one should go to a solitary place;
through the mere recitation of <s>mantras</s>,
the cheating of death occurs.
One should first utter the syllable '<s>ā</s>,'
then clearly '<s>ro</s>' and '<s>lik</s>';
this is called <s>Trailokyavijaya</s> (Conqueror of the Three Worlds),
as taught in the <s>Vidyādhara Piṭaka</s> (Collection of Knowledge-Holders).
One should recite the <s>mantra</s> of this <s>Lokeśvara</s>
one hundred thousand times per syllable;
the faithful one, before that [image], will surely
attain the cheating of death.
Having first uttered '<s>Vairocana</s>,'
then one should say '<s>Tāre</s>' twice,
'<s>Tuttāre</s>' twice, '<s>Ture</s>' twice,
ending with '<s>Svāhā</s>' — [this is] the death-cheating [<s>mantra</s>].
Having recited the <s>mantra</s> taught in the <s>Tārābhyudaya Tantra</s>
one hundred thousand times per syllable,
before [an image of] noble <s>Tārā</s>,
preceded by offerings of curds, honey, and fire —
through <s>homa</s> of ten thousand [offerings of] <s>dūrvā</s> grass,
coral, and [grass from] the northeast direction,
one may avert even death arising
from the power of previous <s>karma</s>.
Beginning with '<s>Oṃ</s>', then '<s>ruru</s>,' after that
the word '<s>sphuru</s>,' then beyond that
'<s>jvala</s>', '<s>tiṣṭha</s>', and likewise '<s>siddha</s>'
— three words: '<s>locaneti</s>';
'<s>sarvārthasādhani svāhā</s>' —
this <s>mantra</s>, written on a pure <s>aśoka</s> leaf
by teachers [to whom] due offering (<s>dakṣiṇā</s>) has been given,
in sandal-paste ink —
recited a hundred thousand or even ten million times,
purified through the method of faith,
washed with waterless [i.e. pure] milk,
and offered into fire with <s>dūrvā</s> grass and the like —
this certainly becomes
a complete cheater of death,
and also becomes a pacifier
of all collections of diseases.
The <s>mantra</s> known as the Noble Hundred-Syllable [<s>mantra</s>],
taught in the <s>Mahāmaṇḍalakalpa</s>,
possessing inconceivable power,
with power witnessed many times —
through recitation of it one hundred thousand times
in the manner of the <s>Bhadracaryā Samādāna</s> (Vow of Good Conduct),
even liberation surely arises;
how much more so, the cheating of death!
First, 'Homage to the <s>Tathāgatas</s>
of the three times'; then
'<s>sarvatrāpratihatāvāpti</s>-
<s>dharmate</s>' — that is the word; then —
after the word '<s>balinām</s>', '<s>Oṃ</s>,'
then the word '<s>asamasama</s>';
'<s>samantato 'nantatāvāpti</s>-
<s>śāsanī</s>' — that is the word; then —
'<s>hara hara smara smara</s>,'
after the word '<s>vigatarāga</s>';
then '<s>buddhadharmate</s>,' followed by
'<s>sara sara samabalā</s>';
two [syllables] '<s>ha</s>' and two [groups of] three;
'<s>gaganamahāvara</s>'
'<s>lakṣaṇe jvala jvalana</s>'
'<s>sāgare</s>' — that word follows;
and having added '<s>svāhā</s>' at the end,
the hundred-syllable <s>mantra</s> is complete;
it is proclaimed as the heart-essence
of all the <s>Tathāgatas</s>.
Through recitation of the <s>Āryamahāpratisarā</s>
<s>mantra</s> one hundred thousand times,
with <s>homa</s> [offerings] of <s>dūrvā</s> grass as one-tenth [of the recitations],
the cheating of death will surely result.
Having said '<s>Oṃ</s>,' then the word '<s>vimale</s>,'
then '<s>jaya vare</s>', followed by '<s>amṛte</s>';

children.text: hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ tataḥ svāhā
children.translated_text: '<s>Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Phaṭ</s>' — then '<s>Svāhā</s>'
should be uttered immediately after.
After '<s>Vairocana</s>', say '<s>bhara</s>' twice,
then utter '<s>saṃbhara</s>' twice;
having said the word '<s>indriyabala</s>',
one should say the word '<s>viśodhani</s>';
'<s>Hūṃ Hūṃ ruru cale Svāhā</s>' —
this <s>mantra</s> cheats death;
it is the heart-essence of <s>Āryamahāpratisarā</s>,
the bestower of all <s>siddhis</s> (attainments).
Having recited the ten-syllable <s>mantra</s>
known as <s>Mṛtyuñjaya</s> (Conqueror of Death)
ten hundred thousand times, one should then perform <s>homa</s>
with white flowers,
anointed with ghee, numbering one hundred thousand,
before the teacher of <s>Lokeśvara</s>;
then, through the power of the <s>mantra</s>, the cheating of death
will certainly occur.
Beginning with '<s>Oṃ</s>', then the syllable '<s>āṃ</s>,'
then the syllable '<s>īṃ</s>' after that;
'<s>ūṃ oṃ mṛtyuñjaya oṃ</s>' —
this is the ten-syllable <s>mantra</s>.
Those <s>mantras</s> which were proclaimed by the <s>Tathāgatas</s>
for the purpose of sustaining life from the beginning of the <s>kalpa</s> (eon),
by which long life is accomplished —
that long [life] is the cheating of death.
By whichever <s>mantras</s> <s>śāntikarma</s> (pacification rites) [are performed],
by those there is increase of lifespan;
and by whichever there is increase of lifespan,
by those there is cheating of death.
Regarding the power of <s>mantras</s> too,
no reasonable doubt exists;
the power of <s>mantras</s> is inconceivable —
since it is accepted by all.
And it is said:
There is no thing in the world
that cannot be accomplished through <s>mantras</s>;
<s>mantras</s> are like wish-fulfilling gems
when applied with proper faith.
Either by the methods prescribed in the <s>kalpas</s> (ritual manuals)
or by application according to one's desire,
in a region where hunger is prevalent,
one should practice <s>amṛtā</s> (the immortal elixir) continually.
Either alone or always combined
with other medicines;
then, having become firm in body,
one does not see the gate of death.
Through the consumption of other
divine medicines as well,
there is increase of lifespan, and through the destruction of old age and disease,
one does not see death.
From a corpse treated with compounds of sky-metal (mercury) and gold,
consumed according to proper rites,
there arises the cheating of death,
due to the nature of the perfected <s>rasāyana</s> (elixir).
Through the conjunction of the new-moon day and similar yogas,
having obtained the intermediate element (<s>antaradhātu</s>),
by the ritual administration of nasal medicine (<s>nasya</s>),
the cheating of death arises.
Through the applications of the five nectars (<s>pañcāmṛta</s>)
as taught in the <s>Saṃpuṭa</s> and other <s>tantras</s>,
combined according to proper instruction,
the cheating of death arises.
One who constantly performs the union of the upper and lower
<s>saṃpuṭa</s> (joining) with beneficial application,
for him, even though enraged, with undiminished splendor,
<s>Yamarāja</s> (Lord of Death) can do nothing.
Even the revival of the dead
has been observed in some cases, through a method
arising from the union of a menstruating maiden and a man,
from the chain [of elements],
with the essences called blood-mixed semen,
not too cool,
or else from drops of essence that have fallen
from one who has just died,
introduced through the opening of a tube smeared with ghee,
by way of emission,
one should convey them through the tip of one's own nose
into the cavity, stage by stage.
Revival has been observed,
and <s>nirodha</s> (cessation) is also praised here;
this yoga, whose efficacy is directly witnessed,
is approved by many.
Either combined or separately,
the <s>triphala</s> (three fruits) combined with <s>āmalaka</s>,
the yogin should constantly practice
the <s>pañcāmṛta rasāyana</s> (five-nectar elixir).
Free from wrinkles and grey hair,
with a body [hard as] diamond and a beautiful form,
one will surely ward off death
even for the count of aeons from the beginning of creation.
This is taught in the <s>Āgama</s> as proven:
through the consumption and application
of many waters and fragrances,
the warding off of death arises immediately.
And through constant practice of these two,
combined with honey and ghee,
one may ward off even death arising
at its proper or improper time.
Regarding the efficacy of medicine,
there should be no doubt whatsoever,
for the inconceivable power of medicines
is seen everywhere.
Having thus diligently performed the external practices
for cheating death according to one's ability,
with apprehension of the great danger of powerful death,
now undertake that which is internal.
Thus ends the Third Chapter in the Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa (Instructions on Cheating Death) composed by the illustrious learned master <s>Vāgīśvarakīrti</s>.
Now the internal
skill in cheating death
is described, by which certainly
death is cheated by the diligent.
In a place free from the dangers of kings, thieves, <s>Māra</s>,
tigers, and the like,
delightful and free from worldly contact,
seated somewhere on a mountain or such place,
eating in moderation, speaking little,
not fond of excessive walking,
sleeping little, meditating much,
devoted to <s>mantra</s> recitation,
engaged in worship of one's chosen deity
and the practice of reading the holy <s>Dharma</s>,
devoted to offering <s>bali</s> at the three junctions of the day
and to the cultivation of <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) and other [<s>brahmavihāras</s>],
thinking "success in one's aims comes from merit alone,"
one should be devoted to meritorious action;
thinking "all success comes from faith,"
one should cultivate ever-increasing faith;
thinking "the completion of what is undertaken comes from effort,"
one should be led by vigor;
thinking "the stability of desired results comes from meditation,"
one should be single-minded in <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation);
thinking "practice comes from renunciation of attachment,"
one should be free from attachment;
thinking "everything comes from right knowledge,"
one should be endowed with knowledge.
Seeing suffering in death
and <s>Dharma</s> in life,
free from all doubts,
one should commence the practice of cheating death.
First, together with meditation,
having recited one hundred thousand [times] the <s>mantra</s> that removes obstacles,
and performed ten thousand <s>homas</s> (fire offerings),
one should ward off all obstacles.
"<s>Namaḥ samantakāya</s>" —
first the words for body, speech, and mind; then
"of the <s>vajras</s>," and "<s>namo vajra</s>-
<s>krodhāya</s>" — one should utter this word.
After the word "<s>mahādaṃṣṭrotkaṭa</s>" (great-fanged and terrible),
one should say the word "<s>bhairavāya</s>" (to the terrifying one),
"to one holding sword, pestle, axe,
and noose in hand,"
"<s>Oṃ</s>," then "<s>amṛtakuṇḍali</s>" (immortal coiled one),
after "<s>khakhakhāhi khāhi</s>,"
the word "<s>tiṣṭha tiṣṭha</s>" (stand, stand), then from that
the twofold "<s>bandha</s>" (bind) and twofold "<s>hana</s>" (strike),
Then:
the twofold "<s>daha</s>" (burn) and twofold "<s>garja</s>" (roar),
then the twofold "<s>visphoṭaya</s>" (burst);
after the word "<s>sarvavajra</s>" (all vajra), one should say
the word "<s>vighnavināyakān</s>" (obstacle-creating <s>Vināyakas</s>).
After the word "<s>mahāgaṇapati</s>" (great lord of hosts),
"to the one who ends life,"
"<s>hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā</s>" —
this is the <s>mantra</s> for removing obstacles.
Or with the heart [<s>mantra</s>] of this very [deity],
one should remove all obstacles;
through recitation and <s>homa</s> as before,
the power of this one is likewise.
Having first uttered "<s>Oṃ</s>," then "<s>hulu hulu</s>,"
then the words "<s>tiṣṭha tiṣṭha</s>" (stand, stand),
the twofold "<s>hana</s>" (strike) and twofold "<s>daha</s>" (burn),
then again "<s>garja garja</s>" (roar, roar),
after the twofold "<s>visphoṭaya</s>" (burst), one should recite
"<s>sarvavighnavināyakān</s>" (all obstacle-creating <s>Vināyakas</s>),

children.text: oṃ amṛta hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ
children.translated_text: "<s>Oṃ amṛta hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ</s>,
protect me, <s>svāhā</s>."
Having thus destroyed all
obstacles of <s>Māra</s>, free from agitation,
one should meditate upon the desired yoga
single-mindedly, day and night.
Peaceful, performing the activities of a <s>Buddha</s>,
dwelling in the dense array (<s>Ghanavyūha</s>),
seated in the bound <s>vajra</s> cross-legged posture (<s>vajraparyaṅka</s>)
upon a lotus and moon seat,
endowed with the <s>bodhyagrī mudrā</s> (gesture of supreme awakening),
with a radiant halo of white rays —
meditating on <s>Vairocana</s> as white,
one does not partake of death until the end of <s>saṃsāra</s>.
Meditating on <s>Akṣobhya</s> and the other <s>Tathāgatas</s>,
rich in their own colors, <s>mudrās</s>, and attire,
with firm divine pride (<s>dṛḍhāhaṅkāra</s>),
one will certainly attain a <s>vajra</s> body.
Within the enclosed moon at the heart,
<s>Lokeśvara</s> (Lord of the World), the imperishable,
peaceful, resembling the moon,
adorned with all ornaments,
bearing in his matted locks the <s>Buddha</s> called
<s>Amitābha</s>, of red color,
seated in the bound <s>vajra</s> cross-legged posture
upon two lotus feet,
with two hands joined in the <s>samādhi mudrā</s> (gesture of meditation),
unperturbed,
accomplishing the aims of all beings,
his form overflowing with compassion.
Meditating in his heart also
upon another <s>Lokeśvara</s> likewise,
and again in that one's heart
another, with single-pointed mind,
until the count reaches ten million —
one should maintain this meditation for that long;
then, with the mind absorbed in the <s>Lokeśvara</s>
at the final, most subtle of the subtle,
seeing this lord of yogins, death
itself dies;
and other faults arising from the aggregates (<s>skandhas</s>)
come to destruction of their own accord.
Seated upon a moon-disc throne
in the center of a white lotus,
seated in the bound <s>vajra</s> cross-legged posture,
holding a wish-granting lotus (<s>varada utpala</s>),
with a form like the rays of the autumn moon,
supported by a moon at her back,
adorned with all ornaments,
with a body of sixteen years of age,
the mother of all <s>Buddhas</s> and their sons,
who assumes any form at will —
meditating on the noble <s>Tārā</s> in the heart,
and in her heart, a wheel of white radiance,
with eight sections filled
with eight syllables,
with the <s>Oṃ</s> syllable at the center,
and the name of the practitioner beginning the hub —
one should meditate with single-pointed mind,
with firm resolve, for six months,
and with unwearied mind one should recite
this ten-syllable <s>mantra</s>:
placing the syllable <s>Oṃ</s> at the beginning,
then one should apply "<s>Tāre</s>,"
then "<s>Tuttāre</s>," then "<s>Ture</s>,"
ending with "<s>Svāhā</s>" — this accomplishes all purposes.
Even by <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Indra</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Candra</s>, <s>Sūrya</s>,
<s>Rudra</s>, the guardians of the directions, and <s>Manmatha</s> (Kāmadeva),
not even the tip of a hair can be broken —
one conquers death like death itself.
The destruction of wrinkles, grey hair, misfortune,
disease, poverty;
the elimination of the eight great fears beginning with lions
and of the milking of suffering;
the acquisition of unsolicited food, drink,
mansions, garments, and the like;
the <s>siddhis</s> (attainments) of the magic sword, eye-ointment, foot-salve,
auspicious vase, and others;
poetic skill, eloquence, retentive memory,
and wisdom entirely pure —
these and other desired <s>siddhis</s>
arise from this <s>cakra</s> (wheel).
Meditating on <s>Locanā</s>, <s>Māmakī</s>, <s>Cuṇḍā</s>,
<s>Mahāśvetā</s>, and other deities,
with their own colors, attire, and <s>mudrās</s>,
one does not see death.
Through the yoga of one's chosen deity indeed,
endowed with firm divine pride,
like a wish-fulfilling gem that accomplishes
all desired aims completely,
resembling conch, jasmine, and moon,
established in the sequence of dissolution,
through unceasing practice of the visualization,
death comes to be cheated.
Having performed the meditation on the <s>Heruka</s> form
as taught in the <s>Cakrasaṃvara Tantra</s>,
through its transformation,
the visualization in skull-cup form,
or the meditation on the skeleton form,
or the visualization of the <s>khaṭvāṅga</s> (skull-staff) —
since one becomes unfit to be killed,
death does not even approach.
From the moon-disc at the crown of the head,
dripping nectar-spray (<s>pīyūṣa</s>),
refreshing the entire body
through all the pores everywhere —
the yogin should meditate for six months,
free from all attachments;
having conquered all diseases,
one conquers death like death itself.
At the top of the head, a white lotus
of a thousand petals, facing downward —
meditating on this with the lunar sequence, one destroys death
and even the [destructions at the end of] aeons.
The meditation on its dark form
with dark-colored rays
flooding [the body],
destroys grey hair and the like.
Placing the tongue against the palate,
with teeth not touching teeth,
through the power of an inconceivable cause,
one should undertake this practice, which is to be trusted on faith.
The saliva-tongue, facing downward,
attached to the upper part of the throat-opening —
one should lick with the tip of the tongue until
the experience of the taste of nectar arises.
Then one conquers death immediately
and destroys grey hair and the like;
protection from all calamities and fears
comes from performing that practice.
Or one should undertake another method
of mindfulness of breathing (<s>ānāpānasmṛti</s>);
through the increase of counting,
one will certainly attain freedom from aging and death.
Twenty-one thousand
plus six hundred
is declared as the count of breaths
of beings in a day and night.
The inhalation of breath is praised,
since it is the accumulation of nectar;
nectar is the means of life,
and by it, death does not afflict.
One should count the inhalations of breath
slowly, in counts of one hundred thousand and more,
with single-pointed mind, according to the method —
this is called the silent recitation.
Through the method of one hundred thousand
silent recitations duly completed,
a person whose lifespan is exhausted will certainly
live for five more years.
From recitation of two hundred thousand and so on,
the increase of lifespan should be calculated thus;
having become skilled in the method,
one should be devoted to the breath-recitation.
One should constantly count one thousand
upon rising in the morning;
freed from all diseases,
one lives for the lifespan of the moon and sun.
One should not remain without practice
nor sleep even for a moment;
having conquered sleep through effort,
regarding food, drink, posture, and the like,
one should direct the breath
in the natural course (<s>anuloma</s>), devoted to breath-circulation;
the yogin devoted to <s>anuloma</s> (natural order)
certainly conquers death.
But the deluded, devoted solely to enjoyment,
die through the reverse course (<s>viloma</s>);
the natural state is <s>anuloma</s> (with the grain),
and <s>viloma</s> (against the grain) is its opposite.
Through the binding of the <s>siṃhavikrīḍita mudrā</s> (lion's play gesture)
and from the retention of breath,
or through mastery of <s>kumbhaka</s> (breath retention) yoga,
<s>nirodha</s> (cessation) cheats death.
Gradually filling with breath
from the soles of the feet to the crown,
<s>kumbhaka</s> (retention) arises from <s>nirodha</s> (cessation);
this is called the method of recitation.
Through the threefold <s>udghāta</s> (exertion) yoga,
<s>kumbhaka</s> is mastered;
the <s>udghāta</s> is considered threefold
according to the division of inferior, middling, and so on.
The designation "<s>udghāta</s>"
indicates the meaning to be explained:
the inferior consists of thirty-six <s>mātrās</s> (units of time),
and the middling is twice that;
the superior should be known as three times that;
by this, <s>kumbhaka</s> is mastered.
Having first performed <s>kumbhaka</s>,
then one's own knee-circle —
touching it three times with the palm
and then giving six finger-snaps —
this is called the <s>mātrā</s> (measure of time)
by the learned, for the purpose of time-measurement.
The <s>kumbhaka</s> practice that lasts
for up to thirty-six <s>mātrās</s>
is considered the inferior <s>udghāta</s>;
the middling is then twice that.
The superior <s>udghāta</s> is three times that,
consisting of one hundred and eight <s>mātrās</s>;
that alone should be mastered with effort
by one who desires to cheat death.
When <s>kumbhaka</s> proceeds to the limit
of the superior <s>udghāta</s>,
then even uninterrupted <s>nirodha</s> (cessation)
becomes very stable.
One who, knowing the day of death,
abides in <s>nirodha</s> (cessation) —
for him, death does not come near
for thousands of <s>kalpas</s> (aeons).
From milking the sky-cow (<s>ākāśadhenu</s>),
an accumulation of dripping nectar,
through a shining <s>maṇḍala</s>
called "vase of <s>Varuṇa</s>" (<s>ghaṭāṅka-vāruṇa</s>) —
the breath issuing from the tip of the nose,
carrying [the nectar], should sprinkle repeatedly
the mind-bee-larva
resting in the drying lotus of the heart.
This meditation of milking the sky (<s>ākāśadohana</s>)
one should practice constantly.
Death, even while seeing him,
does not see him — [for he is] like space.
Or, having abandoned [the practice of] breath [control],
one should always practice reality (<s>tattva</s>) itself.
By reality, death is conquered,
and likewise the other enemies, the <s>Māras</s>.
The complete pacification of all faults,
the arising of all good qualities —
by reality are conquered for human beings
the desired <s>siddhis</s> (attainments) as well.
And reality is declared to be <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness),
which embodies the best of all aspects.
For one who constantly practices that very [emptiness],
death itself is deceived.
Undifferentiated from <s>dharmakāya</s>, <s>saṃbhogakāya</s>, and the rest,
and from <s>dāna</s> (generosity), <s>śīla</s> (moral conduct), and the rest,
connected with all objects of support,
yet devoid of all objects of support,
endowed with the best of all aspects —
such <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness) has been taught by the <s>Jinas</s> (Conquerors).
One should not think a thought that is thinkable;
one should certainly not think the unthinkable.
One should not think what is both thinkable and unthinkable —
then one will attain <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness).
The wise one should not cultivate existence,
nor should one cultivate non-existence.
That which is free from both existence and non-existence —
one should cultivate that, free from both.
Endowed with the best of all aspects,
free from the grasping of emptiness —
one who constantly cultivates [such] <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness)
is not seen even by death.
Death, which arises merely from conceptual fabrication —
he does not see even that.
He does not see the other, manifold <s>Māras</s>,
nor does he see <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence).
Therefore it is said:
'Death is this conceptual fabrication;
in the absence of all things,
[one] is destroyed by one's own conceptualization —
by the sport of ordinary beings.'
Conceptualization is all suffering;
conceptualization is called death.
Therefore one should destroy conceptualization
and become of non-conceptual mind.
Whatever is frequently contemplated
with earnestness and such special qualities,
that becomes vivid and clear,
just as cognitions of desire, grief, and the like [become vivid].
The treatises are indeed easy to obtain,
but the practices [described in them] are very hard to find.
Among people who know the practices,
the practices are not at all hard to find.
One who is skilled in practice, faithful,
established in patience and vigor,
devoted to implementation, and wise —
such a one is a vessel for cheating death.
Through exertion, [proper] cooking, drinking, and the like,
the fire of the belly is kindled.
From the kindled fire [comes] food [digestion];
and its transformation too proceeds according to [one's] capacity.
From transformation comes nourishment of the body;
from nourishment comes increase of strength;
from strength comes increase of lifespan;
from that increase comes long life.
Just as this is established by direct perception for all,
and there is no doubt about it,
so too, from [proper] instruction, there is no doubt
about living even for a <s>kalpa</s> (cosmic age) and more.
A lamp and the like, even when on the verge of extinction
due to the exhaustion of oil and wick,
upon again obtaining oil and such,
endures even to the end of a <s>kalpa</s>.
Just so, this body too,
though dying through old age and the like,
upon obtaining the instructions of the <s>siddhas</s> (accomplished ones),
why should it not endure to the end of a <s>kalpa</s>?
Just as a dilapidated house
endures long through renovation,
so too for a worn-out body —
should there not be [longevity] through renovation?
Nothing is difficult [to achieve] through effort;
therefore, without laying down the burden, strive!
A stream of water, though soft, in time
splits even the surface of rock through constant flow.
Fire is born from wood when it is churned;
the earth, when dug, yields water.
For people of zeal, nothing is unattainable;
all efforts undertaken rightly bear fruit.
Even having learned many
methods of cheating death here,
through non-practice, we have died
smeared with excrement on our deathbed.
And those who are skilled in practice,
learned scholars who have mastered the treatises —
through the fault of non-practice,
they have died baring their teeth [in death-grimace].
Even having known the yoga-treatises
and the many practices,
'Today or tomorrow we shall do it' —
those absorbed in such thinking have died.

children.text: idaṃ kartāsmi śvaḥ punar idam idaṃ cāsya parato
children.translated_text: 'I shall do this tomorrow, then this the next day, and this after that' —

children.text: vṛthā prāptāśvāso vimṛśati na lolāṃ bhavagatim
children.translated_text: vainly reassured, one does not reflect on the fickle course of existence.
Without reaching the end of one's task, fallen into the whirlpool of sense-objects,

children.text: prajā mṛtyor vaktraṃ makara-mukhavan nauḥ praviśati
children.translated_text: beings enter the mouth of death, like a ship into the jaws of a sea-monster.
Thus has been expounded the cheating of the enemy, death,
to be accomplished through <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) and <s>karma</s> (ritual action) established in one's own and others' systems.
It should be diligently arranged out of fear of pitiless death,

children.text: yata iha kamanīyaṃ jīvitān nānyad asti
children.translated_text: since in this [world] there is nothing more desirable than life itself.
The <s>Vajraḍāka</s>, the <s>Catuṣpīṭha</s>,
the <s>Buddhapañjara</s> and others,
the <s>Kālottara</s>, the <s>Kālāvalī</s>,
the <s>Kālapañcāśikā</s> as well,
the <s>Jīvapañcāśikā</s> and other
treatises — having carefully examined [them],
out of compassion for beings, this
instruction on cheating death has been composed.
The autumn-moon sky, perfectly pure —
yet unequaled even by the pure moon of the clear sky —
whatever merit has been attained here [through this work] on [averting] death,
by that may beings be freed from death!
For the ascetic scribes
of the <s>Gaṇanāśrama</s> (Academy of Computation),
the extent of this text is declared to be
three hundred and eighty [verses].

children.text: || iti śrīpaṇḍitācāryavāgīśvarakīrtiviracite mṛtyuvañcanopadeśe caturthaḥ paricchedaḥ samāptaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the fourth chapter of the <s>Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa</s> (Instructions on Cheating Death), composed by the learned master <s>Vāgīśvarakīrti</s>.
